newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sets Sept.14 as date for crucial conference.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sets Sept.14 as date for crucial conference.

text.p: Algerian President Zeroual Liamine on Thursday invited political leaders to a crucial conference on September 14 and 15, aimed at pulling the country out of years of bloodshed and charting a new political future.

The conference, whose dates were given by the official news agency APS, follows months of talks between the presidency and political parties against a background of killings and sabotage, blamed by the authorities on Moslem fundamentalists.
The talks have produced plans to reform Algeria's elections laws, tighten rules on political parties' activity and ultimately ban Islamist parties.
The conference will chart the way political activity will be shielded from the use of violence and religion as a weapon to try to gain power.

Zeroual -- who gambled and won in putting himself up for election as president last November -- is expected to use the recommendations from the talks with political parties, and the results of the conference, to confirm his plans to hold a general election in 1997.
The president has promised that a referendum on the nation's constitution and the country's power structure will precede the general election.

Algeria, an OPEC member with a quota to produce some 750,000 barrels of oil per day, and a major gas exporter to Europe, has had no parliament since the crisis erupted in January 1992 and the then president Chadli Benjedid dissolved the assembly and quit as head of state.
His successor, Mohamed Boudiaf, was assassinated after barely six months in power.
Last month, the presidency and political parties drew up draft reforms due to introduce proportional representation instead of the two round majority system.

The nation's 28 million people used that system to give the Islamists overwhelming victory in local elections in 1990 and take them close to power in the December 1991 first round of the general election.

"The draft law was drawn up in order to ban politicians from seeking more than one mandate and widen Algeria's political representation...It also will open the gate for many Algerians to enter politics," one official said after the working groups produced their proposals.
Algeria's two legal Islamist parties, Nahda and Hamas, will be given a year in which to change their focus or founding principles so as not to run foul of the law.
